title: Introduction to Machine Learning
topicSummary: Machine learning Basics, Foundational theories, Model building, Model training/testing, Model evaluation.

content.text: 1. Overview
This module introduces Machine Learning (ML) as the analytical engine of Urban Informatics.
Objective: Understand how machines learn, build predictive models, and evaluate performance.
2. Machine Learning Basics
Definition: Machine Learning is a subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data and make predictions without explicit programming.
Types of Machine Learning:
Key Terminology:

items: Model → Mathematical function mapping X → y

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: The distinction between supervised and unsupervised learning is critical and often tested. A simple memory aid: Supervised = a teacher shows you correct answers (labeled data); Unsupervised = you discover patterns yourself with no teacher (no labels). Reinforcement = you learn through trial and error with rewards. Urban example: Teaching a model to predict flood levels (supervised — historical flood data with known outcomes) vs. discovering which neighborhoods have similar energy consumption patterns (unsupervised — no predefined groups).
3. Foundational Theories
Machine Learning is built on concepts from:

items: Linear Algebra: Vectors and matrices, data representation.

y = mx + b Used in linear regression to predict values (e.g., traffic vs time).
Loss Function (Error Measurement):
MSE = (1/n) * Σ(yi - ŷi)² 👉 Measures how far predictions are from actual values.

📖 Reading Note: Gradient descent is the engine behind all neural networks and many ML models. Intuition: Imagine you're blindfolded on a hilly landscape and want to reach the lowest valley (minimum error). You take small steps in the direction that feels steepest downhill — that's gradient descent. The step size is the 'learning rate'. Too large a learning rate = you overshoot (model diverges). Too small = you take forever to converge. In urban applications, finding the right learning rate is critical when training traffic flow prediction models on millions of sensor readings.
4. Model Building
Definition: Creating a mathematical model that captures patterns in data.
Steps: Select algorithm → Define features → Define target.
Example: Input (Traffic volume, time) → Output (Predicted congestion level).

📖 Reading Note: Feature selection is as important as algorithm selection. For predicting bus ridership in Hyderabad, researchers tested many features: time of day, day of week, weather, nearby events, holidays, fuel prices. They used a technique called 'feature importance' (available in Random Forest and XGBoost) to rank which features matter most. Result: Day of week + time of day accounted for 78% of predictive power. Weather added only 3%. This helps build lighter, faster models by dropping irrelevant features — a key ML engineering skill.
5. Model Training and Testing

items: Training Phase: Model learns from training data.
Testing Phase: Model is evaluated on unseen (test) data.

content.text: Data Split: Training set (70–80%), Testing set (20–30%).
👉 Key Insight: Training captures patterns; Testing checks generalization.

📖 Reading Note: For time-series urban data (like daily traffic counts), a random 80/20 split is incorrect — it allows future data to 'leak' into training. The correct approach is a temporal split: train on months 1–9, test on months 10–12. This simulates real-world prediction where you always predict the future. Failing to use temporal splits for time-series is one of the most common ML mistakes in urban research papers and is a frequent source of inflated accuracy numbers.

📖 Reading Note: Precision vs. Recall trade-off matters deeply in urban safety applications. For an accident risk detection system: High Recall (catch all real accidents, even with false alarms) is preferred — missing a true accident is worse than a false alert. For a parking fine prediction system: High Precision is preferred — incorrectly fining a vehicle that wasn't violating is a serious problem. The F1 Score balances both. Understanding this trade-off determines how city systems are tuned — it's not always about maximizing accuracy.
7. ML Workflow (Very Important)
End-to-End Pipeline: Data collection → Data cleaning → Feature selection → Model building → Training → Testing → Evaluation → Deployment.
8. Urban Informatics Applications
Example Scenario:
Predict traffic congestion: Input → Time, location, vehicle count | Model → Regression | Output → Congestion level.
9. Topic Connections
How Week 6 Concepts Connect Across the Course:

rows: Week 7 gives the full supervised learning toolkit; Week 8 gives unsupervised — Week 6 is the conceptual introduction to both branches
Reinforcement learning for traffic signal control (introduced as an example in Week 6) is a real application covered in Week 12's smart city systems
Mean, variance, and distributions explored in Week 5's EDA are the exact statistical concepts the ML loss functions in Week 6 are built on
MSE loss function and gradient descent optimization introduced in Week 6 are the core mathematics behind backpropagation in neural networks (Week 9)
Every model from Week 7 (regression/SVM) to Week 9 (LSTM/CNN) uses the train_test_split workflow standardized in Week 6
The MAE/MSE/RMSE and accuracy/F1 metrics from Week 6 are the scorecards used to evaluate all supervised models in Week 7's case studies

content.text: 🔗 Big Picture: Week 6 is the 'ML gateway'. It bridges data analysis (Weeks 2–5) with intelligent systems (Weeks 7–9). The concepts here — features, targets, training, evaluation — are the universal vocabulary for all ML conversations. Weeks 7, 8, 9 are specializations of exactly what Week 6 introduces.

examSummary: Machine Learning = learning from data, not explicit programming
Model building → select algorithm, define features (X) and target (y)
Regression metrics = MAE, MSE, RMSE; Classification = Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1
Overfitting = memorizes training data; Underfitting = model too simple
ML Workflow: Collect → Clean → Feature select → Build → Train → Test → Evaluate → Deploy
